lessons.title: The letters and how they join
lessons.goal: Recognise the 28 letters, read right to left, and see why some words have gaps.

blocks.md: Arabic is written and read **from right to left**. The alphabet has **28 letters**. They stand for consonants (ا, و and ي also spell the long vowels) — the short vowels are small marks written above or below the letters, which you will meet in the next lesson.

Letters inside a word are joined to each other, so most letters have a slightly different shape at the start, middle and end of a word. For example ب (bāʾ) looks like بـ at the start of a word, ـبـ in the middle and ـب at the end. The dot underneath is what tells it apart from ت (two dots above) and ث (three dots above).
**Six letters never join to the letter after them:** ا د ذ ر ز و. That is why some words have small gaps in them. Everything else joins on both sides.

items.note: ب, س and م all join, so the word is one unbroken shape.
د, ا and ر never join forward, so all three letters stand apart.
ٱ and ر don't join to the letter after them, so the word breaks after each of them: ٱل · رحمٰن.

blocks.md: Two more signs work like letters: **ء (hamza)**, a short catch in the throat like the break in "uh-oh", and **ة (tāʾ marbūṭa)**, a t-sound found at the end of many feminine nouns, pronounced -h when you stop on it.

Nine sounds have no English equivalent: ح خ ص ض ط ظ ع غ ق. (ث and ذ are the two th-sounds of "think" and "this".) ص ض ط ظ are "heavy" versions of s, d, t and dh, said with the back of the tongue raised, which darkens the vowel next to them. (In tajwīd, خ غ ق are counted as heavy too.)

quiz.q: Which way is Arabic read?
quiz.explain: Arabic is written and read from right to left.

quiz.q: Which of these letters never joins to the letter after it?
quiz.explain: د is one of the six non-joining letters: ا د ذ ر ز و.

quiz.q: Why do the letters of دَارِ stand apart?
options: د, ا and ر never join to the next letter
quiz.explain: All three letters are non-joiners, so none of them connects forward.

quiz.q: Which letter is the "heavy" s?
quiz.explain: ص (ṣād) is the heavy s. س is a plain s, ش is sh and ث is th as in "think".

lessons.title: Short vowels and sukūn
lessons.goal: Read the three short vowels and the no-vowel sign, and see how they change a word's meaning.

blocks.md: Short vowels are small marks on a letter. The Qur'an always writes them, so every word can be read exactly.
The same letters with different vowels make different words. The three letters ك ت ب are about writing:

items.note: fatḥa on every letter: ka-ta-ba.
ḍamma then kasra makes the verb passive: something was written for you.
The sukūn on ل means the word ends on the consonant, with no vowel after it.

blocks.md: A letter carries **one** mark: a vowel or a sukūn. Reading Arabic is reading letter + mark, letter + mark.

quiz.q: What sound does a kasra (ـِ) make?
quiz.explain: Kasra is the stroke under a letter and sounds i.

quiz.q: How is قُلْ read?
quiz.explain: ق with ḍamma = qu, then ل with sukūn = l: qul.

quiz.q: What does a sukūn (ـْ) tell you?
options: The letter has no vowel after it
quiz.explain: Sukūn marks a letter with no vowel.

quiz.q: كَتَبَ and كُتِبَ have the same letters. What is different?
options: The vowels, which change the meaning
One is a noun with no vowels
quiz.explain: kataba "he wrote, decreed" and kutiba "it was prescribed" differ only in their vowels.

lessons.title: Long vowels
lessons.goal: Read ā, ī and ū, the ending ى, and tell when و and ي are consonants.

blocks.md: A long vowel is a short vowel followed by its matching letter. Hold it for about twice as long.
All three long vowels appear in words from the root ق و ل (to say):

items.note: fatḥa + ا gives the long ā.
kasra + ي gives the long ī.
ḍamma + و gives the long ū.

blocks.md: **ى at the end of a word** (a yāʾ with no dots, called alif maqṣūra) is also read as a long ā:

items.note: و after ḍamma is ū, and the final ى is ā.
The final ى is read ā.

blocks.md: When و or ي has its **own** vowel or a sukūn, it is a consonant (w, y), not a long vowel. In يَوْمِ (yawmi, "day") the ي is y and the و with sukūn after a fatḥa makes the sound aw.

items.note: ي with fatḥa = ya, و with sukūn = w: yaw-mi.

quiz.q: Which letters make the long vowels?
quiz.explain: ا makes ā, ي makes ī and و makes ū.

quiz.q: How is قِيلَ read?
quiz.explain: ق with kasra followed by ي gives the long ī: qīla.

quiz.q: How is the final ى in عَلَى read?
quiz.explain: A dotless ى at the end of a word is read as a long ā: ʿalā.

quiz.q: In يَوْمِ, what is the و?
options: A consonant w (it has a sukūn)
quiz.explain: و carries a sukūn, so it is a consonant: yaw-mi.

lessons.title: Shadda and tanwīn
lessons.goal: Double a letter with shadda, and read the -un, -in, -an endings.

blocks.md: **Shadda (ـّ)**, a small w-shape above a letter, means the letter is said twice: once to close the syllable before it and once to start the next. The letter's vowel is written with it.

items.note: ب has a shadda: rab-bi.
ق has a shadda: al-ḥaq-qu.

blocks.md: A shadda can change the meaning completely:

items.note: No shadda.
Doubling the ل turns "he knew" into "he taught", i.e. made someone know.

blocks.md: **Tanwīn** is a doubled vowel mark at the end of a word. It adds an n-sound:

head: Mark
Sound
Example
rows: -an (often written on an extra ا: ـًا)

blocks.md: Tanwīn usually marks a noun as **indefinite** ("a ..."). The word with ٱلْ ("the") never has it:

items.note: Tanwīn: indefinite.
ٱلْ and a single ḍamma: definite, no tanwīn.
Tanwīn -an on a word ending in ى.

blocks.md: When a reciter stops at the end of a verse, -un and -in are dropped and -an becomes a long ā. So kitābun is read kitāb when you pause on it.

quiz.q: What does a shadda do?
quiz.explain: Shadda means the letter is pronounced twice: rab-bi.

quiz.q: What is the difference between عَلِمَ and عَلَّمَ?
quiz.explain: The shadda on ل makes ʿallama, "he taught" (made someone know).

quiz.q: How is كِتَٰبٌ read?
quiz.explain: The double ḍamma is tanwīn -un: kitābun ("a book").

quiz.q: Can a word with ٱلْ ("the") have tanwīn?
quiz.explain: Tanwīn marks an indefinite noun, so it never appears together with ٱلْ.

lessons.title: ٱلْ "the": sun and moon letters
lessons.goal: Read the article correctly before every letter, and know when the first alif is silent.

blocks.md: ٱلْ (al-) means **"the"**. It is joined to the front of the noun. How you say it depends on the letter that comes next.
**Moon letters (14):** ا ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م ه و ي — the ل is pronounced and carries a sukūn.

items.note: ق is a moon letter, so the ل is heard: al-qamar. This word gives the group its name.
ح is a moon letter.

blocks.md: **Sun letters (14):** ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن — the ل is written but **not pronounced**. Instead the next letter is doubled and carries a shadda.

items.note: Not al-shams: the ل disappears into the ش. This word gives the group its name.
ر is a sun letter.
ن is a sun letter.

blocks.md: Quick check: if the ل has a **sukūn** (ٱلْ) it's a moon letter; if the letter after it has a **shadda** (ٱلشَّ) it's a sun letter.

The first letter ٱ (alif with a small mark on top, called **hamzat al-waṣl**, the joining alif) is only pronounced when you start speaking with the word. In the middle of a sentence it is silent and the word joins onto the one before it:

items.note: بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ is read bismi-llāh, not bismi al-lāh: the ٱ is silent.
يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ: the ٱ is silent, د is a sun letter, so it's yawmid-dīn.

quiz.q: Is ش a sun letter or a moon letter?
quiz.explain: ش is a sun letter: ٱلشَّمْسُ is read ash-shams.

quiz.q: How is ٱلنَّاسِ read?
quiz.explain: ن is a sun letter, so the ل is silent and the ن doubles: an-nāsi.

quiz.q: How do you know ٱلْقَمَرُ starts with a moon letter?
quiz.explain: With a moon letter the ل is pronounced and carries a sukūn.

quiz.q: In بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ, what happens to the ٱ of ٱللَّهِ?
options: It is silent and the words run together
quiz.explain: Hamzat al-waṣl is silent in the middle of speech: bismi-llāh.

lessons.title: Signs only the Qur'an uses
lessons.goal: Read the small alif, the small wāw and yāʾ, silent letters and the pause marks.

blocks.md: The Qur'an is written in a traditional spelling (the rasm) that is older than modern Arabic spelling, with extra small signs added so it can be recited exactly. You'll see these on every page.
**The small (dagger) alif ـٰ** is a long ā written as a tiny alif above the letter instead of a full ا:

items.note: Everyday Arabic writes ذلك the same way, without a full alif.
The small alif gives hā-.
Written with و and a small alif, read as ā. Everyday Arabic writes الصلاة.

blocks.md: **Small wāw ـۥ and small yāʾ ـۦ** after the pronoun ـهُ / ـهِ make its vowel long:

items.note: The small و lengthens -hu to -hū.
The small ي lengthens -hi to -hī.

blocks.md: **ى instead of ي:** the Qur'anic spelling often writes yāʾ without its dots, even in the middle or at the end of a word where it is read as y or ī:

items.note: Everyday spelling is شيء.
Everyday spelling is الذي. Bayan's search accepts either.

blocks.md: **Silent letters** carry a small oval ـ۟ and are not pronounced:

items.note: The final ا has the small oval, so the word ends on -ū.

blocks.md: **Hamza** (the catch in the throat) can sit on its own (ء) or on a "seat": أ إ ؤ ئ. The sound is the same; the seat depends on the vowels around it.

head: Pause mark
Meaning
rows: Pause or continue, both are fine
Pause at one of the two places, not both

blocks.md: Pause marks sit between words and are not part of any word. If you paste a verse into Bayan's search with the marks still in it, they are ignored.

quiz.q: How is the small alif in ذَٰلِكَ read?
quiz.explain: The small (dagger) alif is a long ā: dhālika.

quiz.q: What does the small و in لَهُۥ do?
quiz.explain: The small wāw lengthens the pronoun's vowel: lahū.

quiz.q: How is ءَامَنُوا۟ read?
quiz.explain: The last alif carries the small oval, so it is silent: āmanū.

quiz.q: What does the pause mark ۙ (لا) mean?
options: Pause at one of two places
quiz.explain: لا means "no": don't stop at this point.
